top.line: Ten sgit releases in October turned minutes into seconds; it is time to map what sgit does that Git does not.
top.para: Between 3 and 27 October sgit shipped ten releases, each fixing a bottleneck found by real work. A one-file commit on 76,000 files went from 29 minutes to 4.6 seconds. The ideas came from earlier work on MGraph-DB, Memory-FS and caching. The article maps what Git lacks, what it also has, where it leads, and what is next.

in-short.line: Ten releases, per-command speed-ups, the lineage, and a four-way verdict against Git.
in-short.para: Ten releases fixed real bottlenecks. Commits, pulls and folder clones went from minutes to seconds. The ideas come from MGraph-DB, Memory-FS, content-address caching and the writer pays. Git has no equivalent for encrypted metadata, read keys, blind writes and byte-range folder reads; it does have partial and shallow clones and kept packs, and it leads on merges and ecosystem.

releases.line: Each release fixed a bottleneck a real workload found, ending with pack mode, caches and index packs.
releases.para: The PHP newsroom pushed vaults to gigabytes and wrote field reports; the CLI team reproduced each and released a fix. Early releases fixed the network, middle ones history integrity. Pack mode cut a 1.6 GB clone from 827 to 95 seconds; 0.25.0 a one-file commit from 1,739 to 4.6 seconds; 0.26.0 a pull from 566 to 31.7 seconds, in eighteen hours.

numbers.line: The speed-ups are per command, measured in stated settings, with one regression and a known price.
numbers.para: The newsroom's full pass went from 57 to 35 minutes, mostly capture work, not sgit. Synthetic numbers left the network out; the newsroom's included it. The first status on 0.25.0 took 18 minutes 23 seconds on a slow disk, fixed in 0.26.0. First pushes and compactions are now 35 to 50 seconds slower, paying for the index.

lineage.line: The speed came from earlier work: MGraph-DB, Memory-FS, content-address caching, Type_Safe and the writer pays.
lineage.para: MGraph-DB's two-way cross-references became index members mapping blobs to paths and files to commits. Memory-FS's lesson, read by offset, gave the pack store. Content addresses need no cache invalidation. Type_Safe parsing on reads caused the 0.24.0 slowness, so types stay at the writer. The writer pays once; readers skip the walk.

framing.line: sgit's docs still call it git for encrypted vaults; the comparison should be what Git lacks.
framing.para: The Git framing helped when sgit was young: same verbs, same model. It now undersells sgit, because the interesting parts are those Git does not have. A row-by-row comparison against Git's and GitHub's own documentation gives four verdicts: no equivalent, Git has it too, Git is ahead, and next.

only-sgit.line: Git has no equivalent for encrypted metadata, read keys, blind writes, ranged folder reads and signed shipped indexes.
only-sgit.para: The host reads nothing, unlike git-crypt, though sizes and timing show. A read key is cryptography, usable from any static host, but per vault and not revocable. Append lanes let a sender write without reading. A pack vault folder clone reads only its byte ranges. Index packs travel signed and encrypted. PKI encrypts a file to a person.

git-has-it.line: The memo over-claimed: Git has packs, partial clones, no-checkout clones and shallow clones.
git-has-it.para: Git's packs are delta-compressed and kept whole by default; sgit's differ by being ciphertext on plain storage. clone --path resembles partial clone with sparse-checkout, adding refusal of out-of-scope commits. git clone --no-checkout is old; sgit adds an agent loop. Shallow clones, private branches and signed commits also exist in Git.

git-ahead.line: Git is clearly ahead on merges, staging, identity, storage, ids and its ecosystem.
git-ahead.para: Git merges detect renames and work line by line; sgit merges whole files. sgit refuses partial commits by design. GitHub knows who pushed and keys can be revoked. Git has delta packs and garbage collection, and 160-bit ids by default against sgit's 48-bit format 1. Forges, CI, search and twenty years of stability need a host that reads content.

next.line: Reading one file with no clone and websites served from vaults are designed, not shipped.
next.para: On normal vaults a file is already four plain GETs from any static host. Reading one file from a pack vault by byte range with no clone is Phase 4, not released. PROJECT-003 would move site assets, data and archive into vaults, leaving GitHub Pages only pages, because history grows with generated files; the sites are not near GitHub's limits.

workflows.line: Four jobs are hard in Git and natural in sgit today.
workflows.para: Many agents each clone one folder of a huge vault, with out-of-scope commits refused and nothing readable by the host. A reader gets read-only access to encrypted material with no account. An agent deposits into an inbox it cannot read. An index is trusted only after it is checked against a signed commit.

limits.line: Timings are others' measurements, verdicts are against 0.26.0, and sgit's own docs are partly stale.
limits.para: The timings come from the CLI team and the newsroom and were not re-run. The verdicts compare sgit-ai 0.26.0 with Git's and GitHub's documentation on 27 October. sgit's limitations page still calls signing planned, and its changelog leaves 0.26.0 unreleased. No equivalent means the mainstream toolchain, not add-ons.

sources.line: sgit's release notes, cli.sgit.ai articles and docs, the CLI repository, PyPI, PHP newsroom briefs, Git and GitHub docs.
sources.para: Sources include sgit's 0.24.0 to 0.26.0 release notes, cli.sgit.ai's articles on pack indexes and overhead, its docs on partial clones, history integrity and limitations, the CLI repository's changelog and threat model, PyPI release times, the PHP newsroom's briefs, and Git's and GitHub's documentation. Two figures are cli.sgit.ai's own.
